source: Critical-Questions-of-Thought (CQoT), arXiv 2412.15177 (Dec 2024): steering LLM reasoning with Toulmin-style critical questions
finding: A pipeline makes the model draft a reasoning plan, then checks the plan against 8 critical questions (premises stated, premises supported, links valid, no fallacies, conclusion follows, fits knowledge, plausible). A conclusion is kept only if a majority of questions are answered yes. Then the final answer is written. On MT-Bench Reasoning and Math, scored 1-10 by an LLM judge, CQoT beat both plain and CoT prompts in 18 of 20 comparisons (5 models x 2 tasks x 2 baselines) and tied for best in one.
numbers: Average gain of CQoT over plain: +4.74% (reasoning), +5.71% (math); over CoT: +4.48% and +5.09%; the paper's headline averages are +4.61% reasoning and +5.4% math. Per-model gains over CoT on reasoning ranged from -5.19% (Nemotron-51B) to +12%. Five models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5-pro, Llama 3.1-70B, Nemotron-51B.
quote: critical questions can improve the reasoning capabilities of LLMs
limits: Single LLM judge (GPT-4o, repeated prompting); MT-Bench has few reasoning and math items; free-tier 2024 models; no token count and no equal-compute control, although a multi-step pipeline uses far more tokens than one answer. The questions are generic Toulmin questions, not Walton scheme-specific ones. Per-cell table in the PDF text was garbled, so only the averages and the ablation table are recorded.
agent_relevance: Closest test of critical questions as a checklist (gap 4), but it audits the model's own reasoning rather than a supplied text and is not token-matched. Supports a cheap majority-of-checks gate before committing to an answer; does not show it beats equal-token self-consistency.

source: CQoT ablation and limits (same paper, sections 4 and 5)
finding: Dropping the critical-question stages (keeping only Step 1 plan and Step 4 answer) lowered scores but stayed above the plain baseline, so the questions explain part, not all, of the gain. The authors saw no completely new correct answers: CQoT helps only when the right answer already appears among the model's possible replies. On MT-Bench, plain prompting often beat CoT, especially on reasoning.
numbers: Ablation (plain / Step1+4 / full CQoT), Llama-3.1-70B: reasoning 8.05 / 8.3 / 8.4; math 8.95 / 9.25 / 9.55. Nemotron-51B: reasoning 6.75 / 6.85 / 7.3; math 8.75 / 9.0 / 9.15.
quote: most baselines perform better without CoT, especially on the MT-Bench Reasoning tasks
limits: Only two models in the ablation. The part due to the questions themselves is 0.1 to 0.55 points on a 10-point scale, with no confidence intervals. Pipeline cost not reported.
agent_relevance: About half of the gain comes from the extra plan-then-answer structure, not from the questions. Any checklist gate in our scaffold must be compared with the same extra tokens spent another way.

source: Ruiz-Dolz and Lawrence (2025) An Explainable Framework for Misinformation Identification via Critical Question Answering (NLAS-CQ), arXiv 2503.14626
finding: First corpus with Walton scheme instances plus answers to their critical questions: 3,566 textbook-like scheme instances and 4,687 critical-question answers. Zero-shot GPT-4 and Mixtral answering the critical questions were clearly worse than a fine-tuned RoBERTa. GPT-4 accepted most flawed premises: it answered yes to 53.3% of the critical questions whose true answer was no.
numbers: Confusion matrix (3 runs), true No: RoBERTa-CQA 72.2% right, 27.8% wrong; RoBERTa-CQA with context 74.4% / 25.6%; GPT-4 46.7% / 53.3%. True Yes: RoBERTa 71.1% right, with context 74.9%, GPT-4 79.8%. Counts: 540 No and 846 Yes answers. Mixtral-8x7B was worst. GPT-4 showed no significant change with or without context.
quote: Our generative approaches present a tendency to accept most of the information as valid
limits: Textbook-like machine-written arguments; test set 462 CQs; GPT-4 from 2023-24; prompt details not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 4: a plain LLM asked Walton's critical questions is biased toward yes, so a critical-question checklist needs a forced step that asks what would make the answer no, not a bare yes/no. Same bias toward accepting the text as in the authority results.

source: Ruiz-Dolz and Lawrence (2025), scheme classification in real dialogue (same paper)
finding: Scheme classification is near perfect on textbook arguments but drops sharply on incomplete arguments from real dialogue (QT30 corpus). Grouping the 20 schemes into 8 groups that share critical questions, plus a small fine-tune on dialogue data, recovers much of the loss. The authors conclude that choosing the scheme needs understanding of the argument, not pattern spotting.
numbers: Test sizes: 357 textbook items; 100 QT30 items. Exact F1 values not extracted (table layout garbled); only the direction of the drop is recorded.
quote: the task becomes significantly more challenging when doing so with incomplete arguments uttered in natural language dialogues
limits: Small QT30 set; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Scheme-specific checklists require first picking the scheme, which is the weak step on real dialogue. Supports having the agent state the scheme in the S1 block and allow 'unclear'.

source: Singh, Pathak, Singh (2026) Fallacy Benchmarks Measure Scheme Recognition, Not Fallacy Detection, arXiv 2609.18644 (v2, 20 Sep 2026): benchmark errors and valid class
finding: Fallacy benchmarks pair fallacy classes with one big valid/none class that holds mostly off-topic remarks, opinions and arguments unlike any fallacy. When the shipped CoCoLoFa classifier misses a fallacy, the error lands on 'none', not on another fallacy type, so detection fails while classification holds. Two annotators who sampled the valid classes found almost no correct arguments that use the same scheme as a fallacy.
numbers: 76.9% of errors land on none (95% CI 64.8 to 86.7); TF-IDF baseline 97.1%. Scheme-matched valid arguments in 3 of 183 sampled native none items (CoCoLoFa 1/30, Reddit 1/30, MAFALDA 1/63, Argotario 0/60). Annotator agreement 86.3%, kappa 0.74, Gwet AC1 0.82. Of 25 hand-picked candidates, 10 confirmed. Non-argument share of the none class: 3% CoCoLoFa, 40% Reddit, 52% MAFALDA, 65% Argotario.
quote: What the benchmark reports as fallacy detection is scheme recognition
limits: One group, one preprint, small annotated samples (30 to 63 per corpus). Constructed foils were written by Gemini 2.5 Flash and filtered by a DeepSeek judge.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 and K21: published false-positive rates are low because test sets hold no sound arguments that look like fallacies. Do not read a low benchmark false-positive rate as evidence that our S1 check is safe.

source: Singh et al. (2026), false-positive rate on scheme-matched sound arguments (fine-tuned encoders)
finding: Valid arguments built to use the same scheme as a fallacy but to answer that scheme's critical question (matched negatives, e.g. citing a real expert) were flagged far more often than the native valid class. A control of valid arguments on a different scheme was almost never given the source fallacy label, so the classifier tracks the scheme, not its misuse.
numbers: CoCoLoFa/ModernBERT (5 seeds): native 16.6% +-1.6, matched 58.9% +-2.9. RoBERTa (3 seeds): 19.7% to 70.3%. Reddit within-corpus: 5.7% to 62.0%. Wrong-scheme negatives got the scheme they use 85.9% of the time and the source type 0.4%. Source-type gap matched vs wrong-scheme +40.9 +-1.9 pp. Constructed sets: 655 matched and 738 wrong-scheme CoCoLoFa items after the judge dropped 128 and 58. Human check of 72 matched items by 3 non-author annotators; set impurity 6.9% matched, 22.5% wrong-scheme.
quote: it has learned which scheme an argument uses, not whether it uses it correctly
limits: Matched items are LLM-written, so some (6.9%) are not truly sound. Appeal to nature and false dilemma showed weaker gaps (+10.7 and +19.4 pp single-seed).
agent_relevance: A trained classifier over-flags sound appeals to authority and similar. Our agent should never gate on a scheme label alone; it must also check the critical question (is the source an expert, in the field, in position to know).

source: Singh et al. (2026), zero-shot LLM detectors (Claude Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, Qwen3.6-27B) on the same matched foils
finding: The same dissociation held for three zero-shot LLMs without chain-of-thought. Wrong-scheme sound items were labelled with the scheme they use far more often than with the source fallacy. Raw native-to-matched gaps were smaller and fragile: for Qwen3.6-27B the raw gap was zero. When the prompt asked only whether the argument was fallacious, the raw gap changed sign for the Claude models, so the false-positive rate depends heavily on how the question is posed.
numbers: Native-to-matched gap: Sonnet 5 +13.5 pp, Haiku 4.5 +12.6, Qwen3.6-27B +0.5 (interval spans zero). Type-specific separation: Sonnet 5 +31.0 pp, Haiku 4.5 +45.6, Qwen +25.5. Binary-prompt gap: Sonnet 5 -7.7, Haiku -33.2, Qwen -25.6. Source-type rate for wrong-scheme items 0.3 to 0.5%. 10,260 responses, 2 failed to parse.
quote: The effect attenuates with capability rather than appearing with it, and no detector escapes it.
limits: Three models, one prompt family frozen before the first call, no chain-of-thought arm and no dialogue-type tag, so the second half of gap 2 (does a dialogue-type tag lower false positives) is not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 first half now has numbers for 2026 models: over-flagging of sound look-alikes is real but prompt-dependent. A binary question about whether the reasoning is actually flawed was safer than naming a fallacy, so the S1 check should ask the binary question first.

source: Singh et al. (2026), appeal to authority and the Touche 2026 negative class
finding: Appeal to authority shows the over-flagging strongly. On Argotario, correctly sourced authority arguments were flagged as Irrelevant Authority 78.8% of the time against 11.7% for the native valid class. The Touche 2026 shared-task negatives (chosen by selection to resemble fallacies) were flagged less than the authors' critical-question-matched foils: selection by resemblance recovers about a third of the distance that critical-question matching recovers.
numbers: Argotario Irrelevant Authority: matched 78.8% vs native 11.7%. Hasty generalization: matched 6.8%, below native. Touche negatives flagged 42.9% vs the CoCoLoFa-trained model's 16.3% on Reddit native; own matched foils 58.9%. Flagged Touche items were called the resembled type 15.1 +-1.7% of the time. Cross-corpus gap 26.6 pp, growing to 56.3 pp when trained within corpus.
quote: selecting arguments that resemble a fallacy is not equivalent to constructing arguments that answer the scheme's critical question
limits: Argotario matched set only 219 items; Touche audit used one classifier.
agent_relevance: Appeal to authority is exactly the case S1 marks. A detector keyed on 'according to X' will call sound expert testimony fallacious. The marked block should record the source's competence checks, not just the presence of a citation.

source: Ballon et al. (2026) Big-Big-SycoBench: sycophancy via valid vs invalid arguments, arXiv 2610.15634 (11 Oct 2026)
finding: Tests whether a model revises a quality score after a valid criticism but resists an invalid one (appeal to authority, consensus, emotion, bare assertion, unsupported claim). 450 artefacts, 5,400 arguments. Across ten models, responsiveness to valid arguments was 88 to 95% for seven models, 76 to 77% for Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3, and 32% for Opus 5.5. Compliance with invalid arguments ranged from 0.2% (GPT-6 Astra) to 95% (GPT-4o).
numbers: Invalid-compliance / valid-responsiveness (percent): GPT-6 Astra 0/88, Opus 5.5 1/32 (100-artefact subset), GLM-5.3 9/77, Kimi K3 13/76, Grok 4.7 20/89, GPT-5.5 22/92, GPT-5.6 Terra 28/90, GPT-5.6 Luna 37/90, GPT-5 57/95, GPT-4o 95/89. Contrarian updates below 0.2% for every model. 12 annotators; 94.1% label acceptance on overlapping reviews; 20 baseline scorings per artefact; a revision counts only if it exceeds the model's own baseline variability.
quote: revise its judgement when a user identifies a genuine flaw, but should resist pushback based on fallacies, emotion, or irrelevant appeals to authority
limits: Single-group preprint; artefact scoring task, not answer accuracy; model names as given in the preprint; compliance not split by fallacy family in the text read, so authority items are bundled with four other invalid types.
agent_relevance: First 2026 measurement that scores both sides: resisting bad pressure and yielding to good arguments. Relevant to gaps 2 and 3: the model that resisted best (Opus 5.5) paid with 32% responsiveness, so resistance and false positives trade off. Our S1 hygiene must be tested on both.

source: Shen, Yuan et al. (2026) LoFa, arXiv 2606.31039 (30 Jun 2026): appeal to authority results and model coverage
finding: LoFa pairs factual questions with fallacy-built arguments and runs a multi-round attack. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 showed the lowest resistance to fabricated authority, which the authors tie to RLHF favouring context adherence. The tested models are Llama-3.1 (8B, 70B, 405B), DeepSeek-V3, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4, with closed-model API calls made May to July 2025. No 2026-generation model was tested, so the weakness is not shown to hold on current releases.
numbers: Appeal to Authority LFR@3 on NQ1: GPT-3.5-Turbo 22.54%, GPT-4 39.20%. Llama-3.1 average LFR@3 59.75 (8B), 70.38 (70B), 77.17 (405B); NQ1 averages 44.95, 60.46, 69.59. Results averaged over three runs.
quote: cognitive deference to fabricated authoritative cues, likely an unintended side-effect of RLHF alignment
limits: The RLHF explanation is the authors' guess, untested. Attack arguments were written by DeepSeek-R1 and filtered by an LLM rubric; swapping the attacker to GPT-4 raised resistance by 3 to 12 points, so scores depend on the attacker.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays partly open: LoFa itself has no 2026 model. The only 2026 evidence on yielding to authority-style pressure is Big-Big-SycoBench (0.2% to 95% compliance across models), which says it varies strongly by model.

source: LoFa (2026), chain-of-thought defence and attacker dependence
finding: Chain-of-thought helped resistance for most fallacy types but not for appeal to authority. This was one model (GPT-4) on one dataset (NQ1), a single comparison with no confidence interval.
numbers: GPT-4 on NQ1: CoT improved average LFR@3 by 7 to 13% for most fallacy types, largest gain 13.16% for Straw Man; Appeal to Authority fell by 1.87%. Attacker swap (DeepSeek-R1 base vs GPT-4 attacker) on NQ1: Llama-3.1-8B 47.98 to 53.48 (+5.50); GPT-4 72.88 to 84.88 (+12.00); DeepSeek-V3 89.36 to 94.52 (+5.16).
quote: CoT generally serves as an effective defense
limits: The -1.87% is small and untested for noise; the authors' reading that CoT may worsen deference is an interpretation. Not replicated on other models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 second half: CoT does not clearly hurt on authority, it fails to help. Treat -1.87% as no benefit and do not rely on CoT alone against authority pressure; add an explicit competence check.

source: LoFa (2026) relation to the LOGICOM debate set-up (Payandeh et al. 2023)
finding: LoFa says its evaluation is methodologically inspired by LOGICOM and extends it to factual questions with ground truth, three-run averages and a new metric (LFR@k). It is a related-design follow-up, not an independent replication of Payandeh's finding that GPT-4 was convinced 67% of the time by fallacious vs 37% by logical arguments. It does show fallacy-built arguments move GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on factual answers.
numbers: Payandeh numbers re-verified in the critique: GPT-3.5 37% vs 29%, GPT-4 67% vs 37% (fallacious vs logical). LoFa does not report that contrast; it reports resistance per fallacy type and a scale effect for Llama 3.1 (LFR@3 59.75, 70.38, 77.17).
limits: Different task (facts vs subjective debate), different metric, no logical-argument control arm, so no direct comparison with the 37% logical baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: no independent replication of the 67% vs 37% figure was found; related evidence agrees in direction. Keep K14 single-source.

source: Chen, Greschner, Klinger, Klenk, Eger (2026) Emotionally Charged, Logically Blurred, arXiv 2510.09695: re-read of the 14.5% drop
finding: The 14.5% drop in fallacy detection F1 is a drop for human annotators, not for LLM detectors. Eight LLMs rewrote fallacious arguments with emotional framing; Prolific workers labelled 1,000 arguments (200 originals, 800 framed). The study has no step that neutralises the wording and re-tests, so it gives no data on gap 7.
numbers: Human macro-F1 0.380 to 0.533 on framed vs 0.563 on originals (14.5% relative); share labelled fallacious 91% to 86%. Added tokens correlate with detection gain, Spearman 0.619 (loaded words add fewest tokens and hurt most). Human F1 by perceived emotion: enjoyment 0.528, surprise 0.464, anger 0.501, disgust 0.461, sadness 0.337, fear 0.283, none 0.437.
quote: fallacy detection performance drops by 5.5% in accuracy (relative) on the binary detection task and by 14.5% in F1
limits: Crowd annotators, one study. The earlier claim K17 wrongly called this LLM detection.
agent_relevance: Correction to K17: the 14.5% shows people lose accuracy under emotional wording. Whether neutralising wording helps an LLM checker, and what it costs in tokens, is untested (gap 7 open).

source: Chen et al. (2026), human baseline for fallacy labelling (gap 5 context)
finding: On original LOGIC-derived arguments, crowd annotators reached macro-F1 0.563 on a 5-type labelling task. The paper says the only prior human baseline for LLM fallacy work (MAFALDA) used just 20 samples. Their figure is a different task and metric from MAFALDA level-2 span F1, so no direct model-vs-human comparison is possible.
numbers: 200 original arguments, 5 fallacy types x 40, aggregated labels; 800 framed variants; pre-quiz mean 3.81 of 5; annotation cost 360 euros; LLM-intended emotion differed from human-perceived emotion in 74% of cases.
limits: Aggregated crowd labels; different taxonomy and dataset from MAFALDA.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: no paper measures model-human agreement against human-human agreement on the same items. Best proxies: MAFALDA single-annotator-as-gold level-2 F1 of 0.09 to 0.14 (K07) and Singh's kappa 0.74 on scheme-match coding.

source: Singh et al. (2026), annotator-agreement figures bearing on label ambiguity
finding: Even with a simple 3-way coding (matched valid argument / other argument / non-argument), two independent annotators agreed on 86.3% of 183 items (kappa 0.74). Agreement on the rare category that matters, scheme-matched valid argument, was only 0.50 specific agreement. CoCoLoFa's own authors found 12 of 237 comments were fallacy-like but valid.
numbers: kappa 0.74, Gwet AC1 0.82, positive specific agreement 0.50 on category A. 12 of 237 CoCoLoFa comments (5.1%) were valid scheme instances written when asked to write a fallacy.
limits: Small sample; coding scheme is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Treat sound-versus-fallacious as graded, with an uncertain bucket, not binary. Gap 5 partly closed: label ambiguity is large exactly where false positives are decided; the model-vs-human same-item comparison is still missing.

source: Carrillo et al. (2026) Talk2AI, arXiv 2604.16935: how fallacies were measured in LLM text
finding: Fallacies were found at the quip level by a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier over 13 categories, with class-specific probability thresholds, in a longitudinal chat study. Rates: 17% of user quips and 14.5% of LLM quips contained a fallacy. LLM fallacies concentrate in fewer types than human ones. This measures answers shown to users, not the model's reasoning chain, and the classifier type is the kind shown in d06 to over-flag.
numbers: 17% of user texts, 14.5% of LLM texts (quip level). 13 categories; Miscellaneous excluded. No human check of the labels in the passages read.
quote: also LLMs can fall into logical fallacies, with rates similar to humans'
limits: Classifier labels unvalidated here; per Singh et al. such classifiers over-flag sound scheme look-alikes, so 14.5% is likely an overestimate.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no study found that measures fallacious steps inside an agent's own reasoning chain, or a self-audit pass catching them. CQoT (d01) is the nearest indirect evidence of a self-check gate.

source: Pan, Wu, Li, Luu (2024) Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? EMNLP, arXiv 2410.15050: cost accounting check
finding: The multi-round schemes (warm-up, CoT, clarification) were compared on accuracy and macro-F1 only. A text search of the full paper found no token counts, cost figures or self-consistency baseline, so multi-round gains are not matched to compute.
numbers: Search for token, cost, self-consistency, majority vote, budget gave only two unrelated hits (a training-cost remark and a deployment-efficiency remark). Earlier-verified numbers: +1.27 to +7.54 macro-F1; improvement in 83.7% of experiments.
limits: Absence in the paper text, not a claim about their code.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: no token-matched comparison of multi-round fallacy checks against single-round with several samples. Plan our own test with equal token budgets.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007) Psychological Review 114(3):704; Harris, Hsu, Madsen (2012) Thinking and Reasoning: attempted access
finding: Not opened. The doi redirected to APA psycnet (paywalled) and the Taylor and Francis article returned only Crossref metadata (title, no abstract, no open full text). No primary human numbers were obtained.
limits: Paywalled; replication status of the Bayesian reading unknown from this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Keep K04 single-source and based on the SEP summary.
